messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ali had always been a man who took pride in his health and physical appearance. As a hairdresser, he spent his days surrounded by people looking to improve their looks, and he took inspiration from their transformations. But everything changed when he was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that left him fighting for his life. The experience of undergoing medical procedures, waking up from nightmares, and seeing photos related to the treatment still haunted him today. Every time he saw a photo of himself in the hospital bed, Ali's body would tense up, his heart racing as if he was back in that vulnerable state. He couldn't explain why these visual triggers had such power over him, but they made him feel like he was constantly on edge, ready to react to danger at any moment. The smell of antiseptic and the beeping of machines still lingered in his memory, transporting him back to those terrifying days when every breath felt like a struggle. When these memories resurfaced, Ali would feel the same physical pain he experienced during his illness – a dull ache that seemed to seep into his bones. Sometimes, the emotions came flooding back without any clear image or memory, leaving him feeling lost and disoriented. As time passed, Ali began to see his body as an enemy, one that kept reacting as if it was still in danger even when he was safe. He felt like he couldn't trust himself anymore, like his body was working against him rather than for him. This fear of losing control made him certain that he was going crazy – that the reactions he experienced since the illness meant that his mind was unraveling. Ali's fears and negative appraisals only intensified when he encountered triggers. A medical examination or procedure would send his body into overdrive, making him feel like he was reliving those traumatic moments all over again. His body on alert, ready to react to any perceived danger, Ali felt like he was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the next trigger would set off a chain reaction. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Ali found himself withdrawing from his work as a hairdresser. He couldn't bear the thought of being around people who were coming to him for beauty treatments while he felt so broken inside. The avoidance behaviors that started as a coping mechanism soon became a self-reinforcing cycle – the more he isolated himself, the more he convinced himself that he was indeed going crazy. The memories of his illness still lingered, but now they seemed tainted by his own fears and negative appraisals. Ali felt like he was trapped in a never-ending loop, with his triggers sparking memories, which in turn fueled his fear and self-doubt. It was as if the traumatic event had become a part of him, a constant companion that he couldn't shake. The strain on his relationships and career finally became too much to bear. Ali realized he needed help to break free from this cycle of fear and avoidance. He hoped that therapy would allow him to reclaim control over his body and mind, to trust himself once again. But as he sat in the waiting room, clutching his appointment card, he couldn't shake off the feeling that it might already be too late – that the damage had been done, and he was forever changed by the experience of facing death head-on.
